title: Whether record executives shaped the music; dodging royalties; not duplicating Bob Wills
summary: No one dictated to the Doughboys. Boyd and the band renamed songs to avoid royalties, flops like Beautiful Ohio were dropped, and they avoided repeating tunes Bob Wills did.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: well identify it again here we are on reel three this is a lucky parker interview uh did you do you have any idea uh as uh we know that the music was changing during this period it was changing from uh from a home music of a small band until to a large orchestra do you feel that the a and r men or the company executives played any role in this uh uh no

! ! ! we were always keenly alert to any influences coming in and uh sometimes uh we had our own ideas but uh they never did uh dictate to us now Eli Oberstein and Bill Boyd I don't know I have no idea what went on behind the scenes there we were just workers with Bill Boyd there just kind of a little side man and never did but in the dobois we uh took our own material and we were the leaders there although Bill Boyd later on made gin mill blues and uh he called it mill blues not to pay royalties and we made a tune called Bill Street Mama you know the famous old pop piece and called it Broadway Mama so they wouldn't pay royalties stuff And he called Tin Ruff Blues, Boyd's Blues, or something like that, but it was the same out in that old Tin Ruff. And all kinds of fake names. But he might have had, I don't think so, even there we had a free hand always. We had no dictation from anybody. I know one time just before I joined the band, they'd made a record of Gloomy Sunday. And somebody wrote Blase on the tape, and it never was released, I know, Gloomy Sunday. And they did Once in a While, and that didn't sound very well. And old Parker Wilson wanted to sing, had some little kid singer, Charles somebody, about twelve years old, had him sing Beautiful Ohio, and that didn't sound worth anything on records. We got rid of it, and we went back to our dirty pornographic lyrics, which sold always. These records had tremendous sales, really. It Makes No Difference Now, I know, was a big seller. And I know that in that instance they were keenly alert to whenever It Makes No Difference Now was somehow finally published and then released to other musicians. And Pistol Pack and Mama, those were both arts tunes. When I say arts, I mean first recorded by Art. Satterley. Satterley, yeah thank you. And Don. First recorded by them. And as soon as they were released for other materials, we were the band that was chosen instead of Bob Wills. And sometimes we would have to be careful not to duplicate Bob Wills. He did Back Home Again in Indiana and we did Little Red Boyne in Indiana, that sort of thing, you know. Boy. And we did Avalon and he did something else. And we could never do the tunes he did and he could never do the tunes we did.
